          Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s October 27, 2025 Notice, 1

American Electric Power Service Corporation, the Evergy Companies, Oklahoma Gas and Electric

Company, and Xcel Energy Services Inc. on behalf of Southwestern Public Service Company

(collectively, the SPP TO Group) submit the following comments in support of the proposal of

Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP) to establish the High Impact Large Load (HILL) and High

Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (HILLGA) processes (together, the HILL Proposal).

The HILL Proposal will (1) establish HILLs as a distinct new category of load; (2) create enhanced

study requirements to assess each HILL’s impact to ensure continued reliability of the

Transmission System,” 2 and (3) set forth new operational requirements for HILLs to guarantee

continued system reliability, 3 while the HILLGA process is designed to provide an optional

process “to facilitate the prompt interconnection of generating Resources that are specifically

identified for and limited to serving a HILL.” 4

          The HILL Proposal is overwhelmingly supported by SPP stakeholders for several good

reasons. First and foremost, it will allow utilities in the SPP region to swiftly and reliably meet

the unprecedented acceleration of energy demand from large load customers, including data

Second, the HILL Proposal provides that HILLs may be supplied by grid-connected generation.

Third, at the same time, the HILL Proposal requires new large loads to shoulder appropriate costs,

including the special study costs necessary to accelerate the reliable interconnection of HILLs.

More importantly, HILLs will be charged full transmission rates, which appropriately reflects a

HILL’s reliance on the system as a whole for reliable service and prevents unreasonable cost-shifts

to existing network load. The review process will remain lean and focused because, like new

generation facilities under SPP’s Expedited Resource Adequacy Study (ERAS), HILLs are also

required to make significant up-front deposits that will deter speculative requests. 6 Fourth, these

heightened submission and eligibility requirements for HILLGA Requests, in addition to the fact

that HILLGA Requests are studied in an entirely separate process from SPP’s Definitive

Interconnection System Impact Study (DISIS), together ensure that HILLGA Requests will not

disadvantage existing SPP Interconnection Customers. The Commission should accept the HILL

Proposal because it is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential, 7 and is

consistent with the Administration’s goals of accelerating the connection of large loads.

 I.        BACKGROUND

          A.      The Need for the HILL Proposal

          As SPP has detailed in this and other recent filings, 8 SPP is experiencing “unprecedented”

growth in large load interconnections, primarily due to the growth in data center demand, 9

especially over the last five years. 10 These large loads pose new and unique challenges to

reliability, and SPP’s existing procedures are insufficient to safely, reliably and timely connect

them to SPP’s system.11 As SPP explains, “current regulatory frameworks, transmission planning

processes, and market constructs were designed primarily for incremental and predictable load

growth,” not the steep peaks currently occurring. 12 Among the challenges large loads pose, SPP

cites: (1) their unique operational characteristics, such as nonconforming load profiles, fluttering

and rapid ramping, and higher sensitivity to power quality issues; (2) the additional stress to real-

time operational reliability and resource adequacy planning, especially in areas already

experiencing constraints; (3) the need for faster deployment timelines for supporting generation;

and (4) SPP’s existing tariff requirements, which currently require transmission service applicants

to provide sufficient generation capacity to serve new load. 13



656, 664 (D.C. Cir. 2017) (quoting City of Winnfield, La. v. FERC, 744 F.2d 871, 876 (D.C. Cir.
1984))); accord Emera Me. v. FERC, 854 F.3d 9, 24 (D.C. Cir. 2017).

2025) (ERAS Filing).

            B.        HILL Proposal Mechanics

           The HILL Proposal represents the first step in a “multi-step approach” to address the

challenge of large loads. 14 The HILL process (1) establishes HILLs as a new category of load, (2)

creates enhanced study requirements for those HILLs, and (3) imposes new operational

requirements for HILLs to guarantee continued system reliability. 15 The HILLGA process

supplements the HILL process by providing a new process for expediting new generation to supply

HILLs. 16 The mechanics of the HILL Proposal are described below.

                     1.    The HILL Study Process

           SPP proposes to create a new category of load known as a High Impact Large Loads, or

“HILLs,” which it intends to subject to heightened study and operational requirements due to the

“unique operational and reliability challenges” that HILLs introduce to SPP’s system. SPP defines

a HILL as:

           A new commercial or industrial load, or increase in commercial or industrial load,
           at a single site connected through one or more shared Points of Interconnection
           (POIs) or delivery points, where such load is either (1) 10 MW or more if connected
           to the Transmission System at a voltage level less than or equal to 69 kV; or (2) 50
           MW or more if connected to the Transmission System at a voltage level greater
           than 69 kV. An Electric Storage Resource is not considered a HILL. A load may
           be categorized as a HILL after the initial effective date of Attachment BA of the
           Tariff. High Impact Large Loads must register as such in accordance with
           Attachment AE of the Tariff and follow the processes specified in Attachment BA
           of the Tariff. 17

           The HILL study process is set forth in Attachment BA of the HILL Proposal. The HILL

study process does not, standing alone, result in a grant of transmission service. 18 Transmission

System and begin receiving service. 19 The HILL process adds studies, beyond those already

memorialized in Attachments AQ, AX, and/or Z1, that must be completed by a Network or

Transmission Customer seeking to add or modify a delivery point associated with a HILL. 20

          Before a Transmission Customer can modify a delivery point to accommodate a HILL, a

HILL Delivery Point Study (HDPS) must be conducted to confirm that SPP’s system can control

any disturbances created by the HILL at the Point of Interconnection (POI). HDPSs are more

stringent than the analyses under Attachments AQ and AX and use transient stability assessments

and system strength screening. 21 SPP will perform a supplemental Electromagnetic Transient

(EMT) study if it identifies weaknesses to the system caused by a HILL. 22

          A Transmission Customer must complete an HDPS Agreement that commits a

Transmission Customer to pay certain study costs before starting an HDPS. 23 Among those costs,

SPP proposes a $10,000 non-refundable application fee, adjusted every three years to account for

inflation, as well as a study deposit of $100,000. 24 If SPP determines that an EMT study is

required, an additional study deposit of $200,000 may also be required. 25 If the study costs are

less than the study deposits, SPP will refund any excess deposit funds; on the other hand, the

          To ensure that HILLs do not hinder reliability, HILLs must comply with key reliability

requirements established in SPP’s tariff such as its Integrated Marketplace Market Protocols,

including all Non-Conforming Load requirements, 28 its Phasor Measurement Unit requirements, 29

and its ride-through requirement guidelines. 30

                  2.      The HILLGA Study Process

                          a.    Eligibility

          SPP also proposes an optional, expedited study process designed to promptly interconnect

new Generating Facilities or review and approve a change to an existing Generating Facility for

the limited purpose of serving a HILL. 31 The HILLGA study process is set forth in Attachment

BB of the HILL Proposal. HILLGA requests are serially studied outside of SPP’s existing

generator interconnection process and are used solely to identify how the connecting Generating

Facility will impact grid reliability. 32     The HILLGA process will not result in a grant of

transmission service from the Generating Facility to the HILL but it enables the HILL to seek

HILL. 33

          Unlike the DISIS process, SPP will accept a HILLGA Request at any time. 34 HILLGA

Request submission requirements are similar to, but more stringent than, the DISIS process. The

HILLGA Customer must submit:

          (1) an executed HILLGA Study Agreement; (2) a nonrefundable application fee of
          $20,000; (3) a study deposit of $250,000 for HILLGA Requests up to 500 MW or
          a study deposit of $500,000 for HILLGA Requests over 500 MW; (4)
          demonstration of Site Control; (5) definitive POI; (6) Nameplate Capacity,
          Maximum Injection Capability, and Network Resource Deliverability (MW)
          pursuant to Appendix 1, Attachment A of Attachment BB; (7) Security deposit
          equal to $8,000/MW of the requested Maximum Injection Capability (“Financial
          Security One”); (8) reasonable evidence of satisfaction of one of the listed
          development milestones; and (9) if applicable, the charging parameters of the
          Generating Facility that includes at least one electric storage resource, and a
          description of any control technologies that will limit the operation of the
          Generating Facility to the operating assumptions submitted by the HILLGA
          Customer. 35

These more stringent requirements will deter and limit speculative requests. For example, the

application fee for a HILLGA is twice that of a DISIS request, and the HILLGA process requires

double the financial security of DISIS. 36 A HILLGA Customer must also provide evidence that it

has satisfied a development milestone at the execution of the HILLGA Study Agreement. 37

           Additionally, HILLGAs are geographically limited to the same electrical local area as the

HILL, and the POI of a HILLGA Generating Facility cannot be more than two substations away

from the HILL. 38 A Generating Facility may support multiple HILLs so long as no more than five

substations are involved and no more than two existing transmission line segments are used

between each substation. 39

                        b.      Load Limited Resource Interconnection Service

          The HILLGA Customer will not receive NRIS or ERIS service, but will receive Load

Limited Resource Interconnection Service (LLRIS), a limited interconnection service “that allows

the HILLGA customer to integrate its Generating Facility with the Transmission System with

injection rights limited to the HILL it is supporting.” 40

          To obtain NRIS or ERIS service, a HILLGA Customer must submit a separate

Interconnection Request under SPP’s current interconnection procedures. 41 However, SPP studies

HILLGA Requests for NRIS to better understand the impact of a generator if delivering outside

the local area in emergency conditions, which has the additional benefit of providing the HILLGA

Customer with cost information should it later request that SPP study a Generating Facility for

NRIS. 42

           The HILLGA process does not provide transmission service. 43 Short-Term Service or

Non-Firm Point-To-Point Transmission Service are available to Transmission Customers on an as

available basis, while Long-Term Point-To-Point Transmission Service is available after a

Transmission Customer goes through the Aggregate Transmission Service Study under

Attachment Z1. 44 A HILLGA Customer can obtain Network Integration Transmission Service

only after changing its generation injection rights from LLRIS to NRIS or ERIS through SPP’s

standard interconnection procedures. 45

                         c.      HILLGA Study Mechanics

          Study of a HILLGA Generating Facility will include steady-state, short circuit, stability

analysis, and other screenings to determine if an additional EMT analysis is required. 46 SPP will

determine if Network Upgrades are needed to accommodate the Generating Facility in the local

area. The HILLGA Review Period begins when the Transmission Provider receives a HILLGA

Request, after which SPP has 15 days to identify any deficiencies, which the Generating Facility

has 10 days to cure. 47 The HILLGA Review Period concludes when any deficiencies have been

addressed by the Generating Facility, after which SPP has 90 days to complete a HILLGA System

Impact Study. 48 If a restudy is required due to a higher queued project leaving the queue or being

          At the posting of the HILLGA System Impact Study report, SPP will provide a draft HILL

Generator Interconnection Agreement (HILLGIA) to the HILLGA Customer, which the HILLGA

Customer, Transmission Owner, and SPP will have 45 Calendar Days to negotiate. 50 Following

that period, SPP will have ten Business Days to tender a final HILLGIA, which the HILLGA

that SPP file the HILLGIA unexecuted with the Commission.51

          HILLGA Requests are not higher in the queue than DISIS requests. Instead, SPP will treat

HILLGA Requests like existing generators and incorporate them into its Integrated Transmission

Planning (ITP) models. 52 HILLGA Requests thus cannot drive upgrade costs or restudies in DISIS

clusters because they will not appear in DISIS studies until the DISIS models have been updated

to new ITP models. 53 HILLGA Requests will also be studied individually rather than in clusters.54

Any upgrade costs required by a Generating Facility will therefore be specific to that facility and

will have limited impacts on other requests. 55

 II.       THE HILL PROPOSAL IS JUST AND REASONABLE AND NOT UNDULY
          DISCRIMINATORY OR PREFERENTIAL

          A.        The HILL Proposal Allows SPP Utilities to Swiftly and Reliably Meet the
                    Unprecedented Acceleration of Energy Demand

          The HILL Proposal appropriately responds to skyrocketing demand for electricity and

complements steps SPP has already taken to reduce constraints to its system. By addressing SPP’s

own resource adequacy needs, the HILL Proposal serves the dual purpose of addressing the United

States’ national security goals as stated in recent executive orders. 56 The HILL Proposal has the

overwhelming support of SPP’s stakeholders and should be accepted.

          Reliably and promptly interconnecting large loads is a matter of national security. It is “the

policy of the United States to sustain and enhance America’s global AI dominance in order to

promote human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security.” 57 Consistent with

those goals, the Trump Administration has stated its intent to build AI data centers and

infrastructure, “including high-voltage transmission lines and other equipment.” 58 In its Data

Center Executive Order, the Administration detailed steps specifically designed to hasten the

development of data centers, manufacturing facilities, blockchain technology, and other large

loads, such steps including, but not limited to, providing financial support for qualifying projects, 59

establishing categorical exclusions under the National Environmental Policy Act to facilitate the

construction of projects, 60 and streamlining permitting review. 61

           The demand caused by large loads is of national concern and SPP has faced its own

persistent increase in large load interconnection requests over the last five years. 62 As SPP

explained in the needs assessment report attached to its ERAS filing, SPP is experiencing an

“imminent resource adequacy crisis.” 63 In that report, SPP projected a 2030 aggregate summer

deficiency of 14 GW and a winter deficiency of 10.5 GW. 64 SPP concluded that it needed to

connect approximately 3.4 GW per year of accredited capacity between now and 2030, assuming

load forecasts remain steady. 65 The Commission relied on that report in accepting SPP’s ERAS

proposal. 66

          The HILL Proposal is just one of several means, including ERAS, that SPP is pursuing to

relieve its urgent resource adequacy requirements. 67 SPP has tailored the HILL Proposal to satisfy

each HILL’s unique operating characteristics are fully considered to ensure reliable

          The HILL Proposal received near-unanimous support from SPP’s stakeholders. At the

Markets and Operations Policy Committee (MOPC) meeting held on August 21, 2025, the HILL

Proposal received a 95.6 percent favorable vote from SPP stakeholders. 72 Only two of the 89 total

voting participants in that meeting voted against furthering the HILL Proposal. 73 The Commission

should accept SPP’s filing given that clear stakeholder support and the needs that the HILL

Proposal addresses.

           B.      The HILL Proposal Facilitates the Ability to Supply HILLs with Grid-
                  Connected Generation

          The SPP TO Group supports the filing’s requirement that Load Responsible Entities have

sufficient Designated Resources to serve a HILL, 74 and the filing’s procedures enabling the

efficient addition of new grid-connected generation within a certain distance from the HILL load

in order to meet that requirement. This is consistent with the Department of Energy’s recent

statement that “siting a large load near or at the same point of interconnection as a new generating

facility could reduce the network upgrades needed to interconnect only the load or only the

generating facility.” 75 The HILLGA Proposal creates a specific approach, by allowing a HILLGA

Customer to propose a POI that is in the same “local area” as a HILL.

          SPP’s HILL Proposal requires a proposed HILLGA Generating Facility to support the

HILL within its local area and provides several different approaches to interconnection depending

on whether the Generating Facility is or is not connecting to a 765 kV transmission line.76 The

POI of a Generating Facility that is not connecting to a 765 kV transmission line must not be more

than two substations away from the relevant HILL’s local delivery facilities to be considered

within the same “local area.” 77 The POI of a Generating Facility that is connecting to a 765 kV

transmission line, however, must be within one substation from the HILL that it is supporting to

be considered local. 78 The HILLGA process also permits one Generating Facility to support

                   2.     HILLs Will Be Metered at a Full Transmission Load

          It is essential that large loads pay the full cost of transmission if they connect to the

Transmission System. The HILL Proposal ensures that occurs by treating HILLs and HILLGA

Generating Facilities as distinct for metering purposes and assesses transmission service on the

HILL’s gross withdrawals, not net of on-site generation at the same POI. 95 That is accomplished

by requiring separate transmission-voltage meters for the HILL and its Generating Facility. 96 By

assessing a full transmission charge for HILLs regardless of their supply configuration, SPP has

designed a proposal that avoids incentivizing the diversion of large amounts of generation from

the bulk electric system. This is a core component of SPP’s HILL/HILLGA proposal, and is one

that will ensure that grid-supply is developed rapidly to serve new large loads. This feature of

SPP’s proposal was also essential in securing broad stakeholder support for the proposal.

          D.      The HILLGA Process Does Not Disadvantage Existing DISIS Interconnection
                  Customers

of the HILLGA process. SPP is not modifying DISIS to accommodate HILLGA Requests. Rather,

it is “establishing a separate process to support the need to interconnect generation to support

HILLs in an expedited manner without undue preference.” 97 The HILLGA process therefore is

just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.

models used to study DISIS interconnection requests will not be used to evaluate HILLGA

 III.      THE HILL PROPOSAL FALLS SQUARELY WITHIN THE COMMISSION’S
          JURISDICTION

          Interconnecting new large loads raises questions of federal and state jurisdiction. Recently,

the Commission rejected a proposal addressing the interconnection of large loads for trespassing

into state retail authority. 104 The HILL Proposal does not suffer from those flaws.

          SPP has carefully crafted its HILL Proposal to avoid crossing into state regulation and does

not replicate the issues that caused the Commission to reject the recent Tri-State Generation and

Transmission Association, Inc. (Tri-State) submission. There, the Commission concluded that Tri-

State’s proposal regulated retail activities for, among other things, requiring utilities to enter into

agreements establishing terms of energy sales to retail customers, setting minimum load and

energy requirements for retail purchases, and establishing monthly caps for retail energy or

demand. 105 The Commission refused to assert jurisdiction over a proposal that it perceived as

conditioning service based on compliance with terms and conditions of retail service. 106

          The HILL Proposal, on the other hand, does not “dictate certain terms and conditions for

retail sales … to [an] end-use customer.” 107 Indeed, the HILL Proposal largely replicates SPP’s

existing load and generation interconnection procedures except that it imposes even stricter

requirements on HILLs and HILLGA requests. 108 SPP has also added language to proposed

Attachment BA disclaiming any interference with state laws as a result of the HILL Proposal,

stating that nothing in those attachments “should be construed to preempt any state law, including
